To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, and then mapping the binary masks to the final masks. By breaking the task down in this way, the model can better retain low-frequency information and achieve more precise and detailed predictions. Moreover, the inclusion of a second jump connection enables the model to better integrate both high- and low-frequency information, resulting in a substantial improvement in the accuracy of nucleus detection and counting.
